query: Consider the following context: The combination of elevated temperature and tribo-corrosion leads to the accelerated degradation of structural components used in many extreme environments. Recently developed high-entropy alloys (HEAs) with multiple principal elements have the potential for superior degradation resistance compared with presently used structural alloys. In that context, which material can be used for superior tribo-corrosion degradation resistance, and why?

generation.hypothesis: Under tribo-corrosive conditions at elevated temperature, an equiatomic CoCrFeMnNi high-entropy alloy will exhibit superior resistance compared to conventional single-principal-element alloys due to its stable passivating oxide layer formation.
generation.material_initial_state: Arc- or induction-melted equiatomic CoCrFeMnNi alloy in solution-annealed condition with a polished surface finish
generation.intervention: Subject the CoCrFeMnNi alloy to tribo-corrosion testing in an elevated-temperature saline environment, using a reciprocating contact test configuration
generation.conditions: Temperatures of approximately 500–700 °C; constant normal load; reciprocating wear in a neutral salt solution for a defined time period
generation.structural_mediator: Stable and robust passivating oxide layer formed by the multiple principal elements (especially Cr and Ni)
generation.mechanism: High configurational entropy and sluggish diffusion promote a uniform, adherent oxide film that mitigates simultaneous mechanical wear and corrosion
generation.predicted_outcome: Notably lower material removal rates and reduced corrosion-induced mass loss compared to conventional single-principal-element alloys under identical conditions
generation.baseline: Equivalent testing of conventional stainless steel or Ni-based alloys at elevated temperature in the same saline environment
generation.boundary: Performance advantages may diminish at temperatures above ~800 °C or in more aggressive chemical environments, where oxide films become unstable
generation.uncertainty: Further studies are needed to quantify specific wear rates and confirm the durability of the passivating layer for longer exposures or under different contact loads

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare comparable test coupons of CoCrFeMnNi and a reference alloy (e.g., 304 stainless steel). Subject both to identical reciprocating tribo-corrosion tests at 600 °C in a saline solution for 48 hours. Measure cumulative mass loss and characterize surfaces by microscopy and chemical analysis.
measurements: Coefficient of friction over testing duration
Profilometry and microscopy to assess wear track depth and extent
Composition and thickness of oxide/tribofilm layers
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the CoCrFeMnNi sample does not exhibit lower combined wear and corrosion (less than a 10% improvement in measured mass loss compared to reference) under identical test conditions, the hypothesis is refuted.

cited_evidence.text:
Corrosion resistance of alloys in light water reactors (LWRs) and more generally in oxidative environments is achieved by the formation of protective oxide layers that hinder further oxidation. Alloys containing Cr, Al, or Si typically tend to form a compact and self-healing chromia (Cr 2 O 3 ), alumina (Al 2 O 3 ) or silica (SiO 2 ) layers, respectively, which acts as effective diffusion barriers against further oxidation [1] – [3] . However, in molten fluoride salts (salt of choice for many molten salt reactor concepts, MSRs) these protective oxide layers on structural alloys are unstable which in turn leads to the dissolution of the least noble element in the alloy. Such a corrosion mechanism can lead to a reduction in components’ wall thickness and eventually the loss of the structural integrity of the reactor components [1] , [2] . The dissolution products themselves may lead to plate-out in the relatively cooler sections of the system due to the strong sensitivity of solubility of analytes to temperature.

Development of materials suitable for molten fluoride salt environments started in the 1950s with the Aircraft Reactor Experiment (ARE) [4] . This experiment used Inconel 6

Unlike other conventional alloys based on a “principal element,” high-entropy alloy (HEA) is a unique material that maintains a random solid solution structure without forming intermetallic compounds in operating temperatures due to its high configurational entropy [1] – [3] . It also has outstanding physical and chemical properties, which makes it a potential replacement for traditional metallic materials, and it has recently been referred to as a multi-principal element alloy (MPEA) or compositionally concentrated alloy (CCA) [4] – [9] .

As attention in HEAs increases, many studies have been conducted to explore its mechanical, physical and chemical properties [10] – [15] . In particular, equiatomic CoCrFeMnNi HEA, which was the first developed HEA, is the most studied because of its excellent combination of tensile strength and elongation along with excellent fracture toughness and corrosion resistance [6] , [16] – [21] . However, despite the advantages of equiatomic CoCrFeMnNi HEA, many issues arise owing to its low yield strength and costly and complex thermomechanical processing (i.e., multiple casting → hot rolling → homogenization → cold rolling → annealing → cutting, etc.
